title: Three States and More
intro: A 3D view of third-order systems: fast and slow modes, dominant poles, repeated poles, and a first look at the Lorenz system. Two states fit on a sheet of paper; three need a box, and most real systems need more. This page keeps the same ideas and watches them play out with three states: which modes there are, which of them matter, and what you can throw away.

blocks.text: From two states to n

Nothing in the state equation cares how many states there are. With $n$ states, $x$ is a column of $n$ numbers, $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, and the solution is still $x(t) = e^{At}x(0)$ for a free response. The poles are the $n$ roots of $\det(sI - A) = 0$, a polynomial of degree $n$, and the system is asymptotically stable exactly when every one of them has a negative real part. A system with $n$ states is a point moving in $n$-dimensional space. We cannot draw that for $n > 3$, but the three-state viewer on this page shows everything that is new about $n = 3$, and the rest is bookkeeping.

What does change is the variety. With two states a pole pair is either two real numbers or one complex pair. With three states there is always one more pole, and it has to be real. The reason: $\det(sI - A)$ has real coefficients, so its complex roots come in conjugate pairs, and a cubic cannot be made of pairs alone. (Another way to see it: a real cubic goes to $-\infty$ at one end and $+\infty$ at the other, so it must cross zero somewhere.) The same is true for every odd $n$. So a third-order system has either three real poles (two or all three of them may be equal, a repeated pole) or one real pole and a complex pair.

Each real pole $\lambda$ is a straight-line mode, a direction $v$ with $Av = \lambda v$ along which the state moves like $e^{\lambda t}v$. A complex pair is a plane in which the state turns and grows or shrinks. These are the modes met on Modes and Stability (#/math/state-space/modes-and-stability), and the picture is the one from Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues). The whole solution is the sum of the modes, weighted by where you start. If $A = P\Lambda P^{-1}$, the columns of $P$ are the eigenvectors $v_i$ and the rows of $P^{-1}$ are the left eigenvectors $w_i^{\top}$, with $w_i^{\top}v_j = 1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise. Then

blocks.tex: x(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( w_i^{\top} x(0) \right) e^{\lambda_i t}\, v_i

blocks.text: This is modal decomposition: split the start into its pieces along the eigenvectors, let each piece evolve by itself, and add the pieces back. The number $w_i^{\top}x(0)$ says how much of mode $i$ the start contains. It is the same formula as $A^k = P\Lambda^k P^{-1}$ on Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation), in continuous time. The rest of this page does it for real systems.
The 3D viewer

The viewer draws the state's path in a box with a floor grid. The dark curve is the path from the start $x(0)$ (the circle), and the faint curve on the floor is its shadow. The three axes are $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$. Dashed lines through the resting point are the real eigen-directions, each labelled with its $\lambda$, and an amber disc marks the plane of a complex pair. Below, $x_1$ is blue, $x_2$ amber, $x_3$ violet and the output $y$ a thick red line, against time, and next to them the poles and zeros in the $s$-plane. The Turn and Tilt sliders, or a drag on the picture, rotate the view. Next step ▶ gives an eight-step walk-through, and Play ▶ draws the path as time runs. The first example below has its own copy of the viewer; every viewer on this page works on its own.
A spring pushed through a slow actuator

Take the mass on a spring from the first topic page, $m = 1$, $k = 4$, but with only $c = 0.4$ of damping, and suppose we cannot push it directly. The force $x_3$ on the mass comes from an actuator that follows the command $u$ with a lag: $x_3' = -5x_3 + 5u$, which means the actuator reaches its target in a time constant of $1/5 = 0.2$ s. The three states are position $x_1$, velocity $x_2$ and actuator force $x_3$:

blocks.tex: \begin{pmatrix} x_1' \\ x_2' \\ x_3' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & -0.4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix} u, \qquad y = x_1

blocks.text: The bottom row has a single non-zero entry, so $x_3$ obeys its own equation and does not care about the other two. A matrix with this shape (block triangular) has the poles of its diagonal blocks. The upper block $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & -0.4 \end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $s^2 + 0.4s + 4$, with roots $-0.2 \pm 1.99j$, and the lower block gives $s = -5$. Multiplying out, $\det(sI - A) = (s^2 + 0.4s + 4)(s + 5) = s^3 + 5.4s^2 + 6s + 20$, which is exactly the denominator of the transfer function the viewer prints.

Now the modes. For $\lambda = -5$ solve $(A + 5I)v = 0$. The rows are $5v_1 + v_2 = 0$, then $-4v_1 + 4.6v_2 + v_3 = 0$, and the last row is $0 = 0$. So $v_2 = -5v_1$ and $v_3 = 4v_1 - 4.6v_2 = 4v_1 + 23v_1 = 27v_1$: the direction $v = (1, -5, 27)$, which the viewer prints as the unit vector $(0.04, -0.18, 0.98)$. The complex pair has eigenvectors with third entry zero, because the third row of $A - \lambda I$ reads $(-5 - \lambda)v_3 = 0$ and $\lambda \ne -5$. So the amber plane is the plane $x_3 = 0$, the position-velocity plane.

Start at the viewer's default $x(0) = (1, 0, 1)$. The left eigenvector for $\lambda = -5$ is $w^{\top} = (0, 0, 1/27)$ (check: $w^{\top}v = 27/27 = 1$, and $w^{\top}A = (0, 0, -5/27) = -5w^{\top}$). So the fast mode carries $w^{\top}x(0) = 1/27 = 0.037$ of the start. What is left over is $x(0) - \tfrac{1}{27}(1, -5, 27) = (26/27, 5/27, 0) = (0.963, 0.185, 0)$, which lies in the plane and spirals in slowly, with envelope $e^{-0.2t}$. In short,

blocks.tex: x(t) = \tfrac{1}{27}\,e^{-5t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ 27 \end{pmatrix} + e^{-0.2t}\,(\text{a spiral in the plane } x_3 = 0)

blocks.text: The first term is gone after about a second (at $t = 0.2$ s, $x_3 = e^{-1} = 0.368$; at $t = 1$ s it is $0.007$). That is the picture: the path drops quickly onto the amber plane, then turns slowly inside it, once every $2\pi/1.99 = 3.16$ s, and it needs about $4/0.2 = 20$ s to settle within 2%.

widget.title: A spring behind a slow actuator

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: Leave the viewer on its default, the spring with a slow actuator, $x(0) = (1, 0, 1)$. Look at the violet curve $x_3$ below: it falls from 1 to almost 0 in a second (it is $e^{-5t}$), while blue $x_1$ and amber $x_2$ swing like a lightly damped spring, about one swing every 3.2 s. In the 3D box the path starts above the amber disc and comes down onto it within the first second. Press Next step ▶ four times: step 4 says that the fastest mode dies away with time constant 0.2 s and the slowest with 5 s, so the path first drops quickly onto the amber plane. The readout ends 'At t = 25 s: x = (0.01, 0.01, 0.00), y = 0.005', and the poles are printed as '−0.2 ± 1.99j and −5'.
Model reduction: keep the dominant poles

A fast mode that dies in a second is hardly visible after that, and a designer often drops it. The poles nearest the imaginary axis, here $-0.2 \pm 1.99j$, are the dominant poles: they set the long-term behaviour. To drop the actuator, treat it as instant. Its steady state is $x_3 = u$ (set $x_3' = 0$ in $x_3' = -5x_3 + 5u$), so the spring sees the force $u$ directly, and the model collapses to a plain mass on a spring with $k = 4$ and $c = 0.4$,

Both have the steady-state gain $G(0) = 5/20 = 1/4$, so they settle on the same final value, 0.25, and both have the same slow poles. They differ in how they get there. The unit step response of the full system peaks at 0.419 at $t = 1.78$ s; the reduced one peaks at 0.432 at $t = 1.58$ s. The two curves are never further apart than 0.080 (at $t = 0.93$ s, on a swing of about 0.4), and the gap shrinks as the swing dies, to under 0.025 after 6 s and under 0.01 after 12 s. The reduced model is early by about 0.2 s, the time constant of the actuator it forgot: delaying the reduced response by 0.2 s brings it within 0.02 of the full one. Whether that is good enough depends on the use. For judging the final value and the ringing it is fine; for designing a fast feedback loop it would hide the lag that limits how fast the loop can go.

This is the general rule for model reduction: write the system in modes, keep the slow ones, and replace each fast mode by its steady state (here a gain of 1), remembering that the fast mode leaves a small delay behind. It works when the poles are well separated, five times or more, as here ($5$ against $0.2$). It fails when they are not.
Real poles: a motor with its current, and three tanks

A DC motor driven by a voltage, with the electrical side included, has three states: the angle $x_1$, the speed $x_2$ and the armature current $x_3$. In the viewer's numbers the angle is the integral of the speed ($x_1' = x_2$), the speed falls with friction and rises with current ($x_2' = -0.5x_2 + x_3$), and the current is pushed by the voltage and opposed by the back-voltage the spinning motor makes ($x_3' = -2x_2 - 4x_3 + 2u$). The matrix has a column of zeros, since nothing depends on the angle, and its characteristic polynomial is $s(s^2 + 4.5s + 4)$. The roots of the quadratic are $(-4.5 \pm \sqrt{20.25 - 16})/2 = -1.219$ and $-3.281$, and the third pole is $0$: an integrator, the angle.

The pole at 0 means a whole line of resting points, $(c, 0, 0)$ for any angle $c$. A free motor settles at some angle, and which one is a modal-decomposition question. The left eigenvector for $\lambda = 0$ solves $w^{\top}A = 0$: the second column gives $w_1 - 0.5w_2 - 2w_3 = 0$ and the third gives $w_2 - 4w_3 = 0$. Taking $w_3 = 0.25$ gives $w_2 = 1$ and $w_1 = 1$, so $w^{\top} = (1, 1, 0.25)$, and $w^{\top}v = 1$ for the eigenvector $v = (1, 0, 0)$. The final angle is $w^{\top}x(0)$. From $x(0) = (1, 0, 1)$ that is $1 + 0 + 0.25 = 1.25$: the motor starts at angle 1 with a current of 1 and coasts on to 1.25, because the current gives it a push before the two decaying modes die away.

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: Choose DC motor with its current (the viewer above is already set to it), with the default start $x(0) = (1, 0, 1)$. Watch the blue curve $x_1$: it climbs from 1 and flattens out. The readout ends 'At t = 8 s: x = (1.25, 0.00, 0.00), y = 1.250', which is the 1.25 computed above. The poles are '0, −1.219 and −3.281: on the edge'. Now set Input to unit step and all three starts to 0 (or press Next step ▶ six times, which does it): there is no red + for a resting point, and $x_1$ climbs forever, because a constant voltage keeps the motor turning.

Three tanks in a row are the same story with real poles all in the left half-plane. Tank 1 drains into tank 2, tank 2 into tank 3, which drains out, with drain rates 1, 0.6 and 0.3 per second, and the input is a flow into tank 1 with the level of tank 3 as the output. A lower-triangular $A$ has its diagonal entries as eigenvalues, so the poles are $-1$, $-0.6$ and $-0.3$, and the transfer function is the product of three first-order lags,

with $G(0) = 0.6/0.18 = 3.333$: the final level of tank 3 is 3.33 times the inflow. The step response comes from partial fractions: the term for each pole is its residue, found by covering the factor and evaluating the rest. At $s = -1$ the residue is $0.6/((-0.4)(-0.7)) = 2.143$, at $s = -0.6$ it is $0.6/((0.4)(-0.3)) = -5$, and at $s = -0.3$ it is $0.6/((0.7)(0.3)) = 2.857$. (They add to 0, as the impulse response must start from 0.) Each $c/(s + p)$ gives a step-response term $(c/p)(1 - e^{-pt})$, so

At $t = 5$ this is $3.333 - 0.014 + 0.415 - 2.125 = 1.609$, the value of the output curve in the viewer at 5 s. It is an S-shaped curve: no overshoot (there is no complex pair), a slow start (three lags in a row) and a settling dominated by the slowest pole, $-0.3$, with a time constant of $3.33$ s. Within 2% of the final value takes about 16.5 s, a little more than the $4/0.3 = 13.3$ s the viewer's step 8 quotes, because the other two lags add delay.

The red + marks the resting point $-A^{-1}B = (1, 1.67, 3.33)$: tank 1 ends at 1 (its drain of 1 per second balances the inflow of 1), tank 2 at $1/0.6 = 1.67$ and tank 3 at $0.6 \times 1.67/0.3 = 3.33$. The violet curve $x_3$ (which is also the thick red output $y$, since $C = (0, 0, 1)$ picks tank 3) rises slowly at first and ends near 3.33. The readout ends 'At t = 16.67 s: x = (1.00, 1.67, 3.27), y = 3.270', still just short of 3.33. Next step ▶ starts the walk-through: step 1 takes the input back to none and sets $x(0) = (1, 0, 1)$, and at step 4 the text says 'the fastest dies away with time constant 1 s, the slowest with 3.33 s'.
A repeated pole: three lags in a row

Three identical first-order lags, one after the other, give $G(s) = 1/(s + 1)^3$. The simplest state-space form for it is the companion form: take $x_1 = y$, $x_2 = y'$, $x_3 = y''$, so that $x_1' = x_2$, $x_2' = x_3$, and the differential equation $y''' + 3y'' + 3y' + y = u$ gives $x_3' = -x_1 - 3x_2 - 3x_3 + u$. The matrix has the coefficients of $(s + 1)^3 = s^3 + 3s^2 + 3s + 1$ along its bottom row, with signs reversed. The poles are $-1, -1, -1$.
Three equal poles do not give three straight-line modes. The matrix $N = A + I$ is

$N$ has rank 2, so the equation $Nv = 0$ has only one independent solution, $v = (1, -1, 1)$. The matrix is defective, which is the situation from Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues). Since $A = -I + N$ and $I$ commutes with everything, $e^{At} = e^{-t}e^{Nt}$, and because $N^3 = 0$ the series for $e^{Nt}$ stops after three terms:

Every entry is $e^{-t}$ times a polynomial in $t$ of degree at most 2. Take $x(0) = (1, 0, 0)$. Then $Nx(0) = (1, 0, -1)$ and $N^2x(0) = (1, -1, 1)$, so $x(t) = e^{-t}\left( 1 + t + \tfrac{t^2}{2},\ -\tfrac{t^2}{2},\ -t + \tfrac{t^2}{2} \right)$. At $t = 1$ that is $e^{-1}(2.5, -0.5, -0.5) = (0.920, -0.184, -0.184)$. The factors $t$ and $t^2$ make the path swing out before $e^{-t}$ pulls it in: $x_2 = -t^2e^{-t}/2$ falls to $-0.271$ at $t = 2$ and then creeps back to 0.

The same factors show in the step response. For $G = 1/(s + 1)^3$, $y(t) = 1 - e^{-t}\left(1 + t + \tfrac{t^2}{2}\right)$, which is 0.080 at $t = 1$, 0.323 at $t = 2$, 0.577 at $t = 3$ and 0.875 at $t = 5$. A single lag with the same pole would already be at $1 - e^{-2} = 0.865$ at $t = 2$. The chain is slower: it takes 5.32 s to reach 90% and 7.5 s to settle within 2%. The viewer's step 8 estimates the settling time as $4/|\lambda| = 4$ s, which is right for one lag and optimistic for three. A repeated pole is the case where the rule of thumb is least reliable.

blocks.text: The viewer is set to the chain of three lags with $x(0) = (1, 0, 0)$. There is only one dashed eigen-line, labelled λ = −1. The path leaves $x(0)$ and curves out before it comes back along that line; amber $x_2$ dips below zero, to $-0.27$ at 2 s, and comes back. Press Next step ▶ four times for 'All three eigenvalues are equal (λ = −1) but there is only one eigen-direction, so the matrix is defective'. The poles print as '−1, −1 and −1', and the readout ends 'At t = 11 s: x = (0.00, 0.00, 0.00), y = 0.001'.
A centre and a decay: a spin about an axis

Put a rotation in the first two states and a decay in the third: $x_1' = -x_2$, $x_2' = x_1$, $x_3' = -0.5x_3$. The rotation block has poles $\pm j$, so $(x_1, x_2)$ goes round the unit circle, one turn every $2\pi = 6.28$ s, with no growth or decay; the third state falls like $e^{-0.5t}$. From $x(0) = (1, 0, 1)$ the state is $x(t) = (\cos t, \sin t, e^{-0.5t})$: a helix that flattens onto the circle. After one turn, at $t = 2\pi$, the height is $e^{-\pi} = 0.043$. The amber disc in the viewer is that plane, and the circle lies in it forever.

This is marginal stability: the two poles on the imaginary axis never die away, so the system settles to a steady circling, not to rest. The input $B = (1, 0, 1)$ pushes both parts and the output is $y = x_1 + x_3$. The transfer function is the sum of the two parts: $s/(s^2 + 1)$ for the rotation (from $x_1' = -x_2 + u$ and $x_2' = x_1$) and $1/(s + 0.5)$ for the decay, which together make $(2s^2 + 0.5s + 1)/(s^3 + 0.5s^2 + s + 0.5)$, as the readout prints. Its denominator has the pole pair on the imaginary axis, so a sinusoidal input at $\omega = 1$ rad/s would drive the output up without limit (resonance), though a step does not: with a unit step from rest, $x_1 = \sin t$, $x_2 = 1 - \cos t$ and $x_3 = 2(1 - e^{-0.5t})$, a circle round the resting point $(0, 1, 2)$.

The path is a helix that flattens onto a circle in the amber disc; violet $x_3$ falls away while blue $x_1$ and amber $x_2$ keep swinging at full size (one turn every 6.28 s: the step-3 text says 'turning in the amber plane once every 6.28 s with no growth or decay'). The readout ends 'At t = 18.85 s: x = (1.00, 0.00, 0.00), y = 1.000': exactly three turns later, back at $x_1 = 1$. Set Input to unit step and the three starts to 0: the red + sits at $(0, 1, 2)$ and the path circles it.
Near the origin of the Lorenz system

The Lorenz system is the famous three-state model of convection that Edward Lorenz studied in 1963. It has the equations $x' = \sigma(y - x)$, $y' = \rho x - y - xz$, $z' = -\beta z + xy$, with $\sigma = 10$, $\rho = 28$ and $\beta = 8/3$. The terms $xz$ and $xy$ are products of states, so the equations are nonlinear, and a state-space model $x' = Ax$ cannot hold them. Close to the origin, though, the products are tiny compared with the other terms, and dropping them leaves a linear system, the one in the viewer:

The third state is on its own, so one pole is $-8/3 = -2.667$. The other two come from the upper block, $s^2 + 11s - 270 = 0$, so $s = (-11 \pm \sqrt{121 + 1080})/2 = 11.828$ and $-22.828$. One pole is positive. Near the origin the system is a saddle in three dimensions: a plane's worth of directions are attracted (the stable direction in the $x$–$y$ plane, along $(1, -1.28, 0)$, and the $z$ axis) while one direction, along $(1, 2.18, 0)$, is repelled. Almost every start is pushed out along the repelling line. From $x(0) = (1, 0, 1)$ the unstable part of the start is 0.370 of it, found as before by splitting $(1, 0)$ into $a(1, 2.18) + b(1, -1.28)$, and it grows as $e^{11.83t}$: by $t = 0.29$ s it has grown thirty-fold, and the state is $(11.1, 24.2, 0.46)$.

The input push is $B = (1, 0, 0)$ and the output reads $x$. Neither touches $z$: a push on $x$ never moves $z$ in the linear model, and $x$ does not depend on $z$. The model is therefore not controllable and not observable. The transfer function shows it: the viewer prints $(s^2 + 3.667s + 2.667)/(s^3 + 13.667s^2 - 240.667s - 720)$ and both parts have a factor $s + 8/3$, which would cancel to leave $(s + 1)/(s^2 + 11s - 270)$, a second-order function with the two $x$–$y$ poles. The viewer leaves it uncancelled and tells you in step 7 that not every mode can be reached or seen. The cancelled pole is the hidden mode from Controllability and Observability (#/math/state-space/controllability-observability).

The three dashed lines are the three real eigen-directions, labelled 'λ = −22.828', 'λ = 11.828' and 'λ = −2.667'. The path shoots out along the line with $\lambda = 11.828$ while violet $x_3$ falls to 0.46. The readout shows 'Poles 11.828, −2.667 and −22.828: unstable' and ends 'Not controllable, not observable. At t = 0.29 s: x = (11.11, 24.24, 0.46), y = 11.105'. The real Lorenz system does not run off to infinity: the nonlinear terms $xz$ and $xy$, which this model drops, take over and bend the path into the butterfly. How to study that is the subject of the next topic in the Math list, Phase-Space Dynamics (planned, not yet written).
Stability of a cubic without finding the roots

For a cubic $s^3 + a_2s^2 + a_1s + a_0$ with real coefficients there is a test that never finds a root, the Routh–Hurwitz condition: all three coefficients must be positive and $a_2a_1 > a_0$. Try it on the five systems. The slow actuator has $5.4 \times 6 = 32.4 > 20$: stable. The tanks have $1.9 \times 1.08 = 2.052 > 0.18$: stable. The chain has $3 \times 3 = 9 > 1$: stable. The motor has $a_0 = 0$, so not strictly positive: a pole at 0, on the edge. The Lorenz denominator has $a_1 = -240.667 < 0$: unstable at once. The spin has $a_2a_1 = 0.5 \times 1 = 0.5 = a_0$, exactly on the boundary: a pole pair on the imaginary axis. The condition is derived in the sources below and listed on State-Space Tables (#/math/state-space/tables). For larger $n$ the Routh array builds a longer test. A stable polynomial always has all its coefficients positive (no gaps and no sign changes), so a zero or negative coefficient settles the question at once; but from $n = 3$ on, positive coefficients alone are not enough, which is why the extra condition $a_2a_1 > a_0$ is needed.
What carries over to many states

Everything above works for four, ten or a thousand states: find the eigenvalues, split the start into modes, keep the slow ones. The number of real poles is $n$ minus twice the number of complex pairs. The practical differences are that nobody computes the eigenvalues by hand for $n > 3$, a computer does (see Solving the State Equations (#/math/state-space/solving) for how it computes $e^{At}$), and that real systems often have a few slow modes and many fast ones, so model reduction (dominant poles above, or the refinements that rank modes by how controllable and observable they are) is the first thing an engineer does. The tests of Controllability and Observability (#/math/state-space/controllability-observability) and the design of State Feedback and Pole Placement (#/math/state-space/state-feedback) and Observers: Estimating the State (#/math/state-space/observers) all work for any $n$ as written.

blocks.title: The final angle of the motor
blocks.text: The DC motor with its current has $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.5 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$ and no input. Starting at $x(0) = (0, 1, 2)$, at which angle does the motor come to rest?
solution: The angle is the state that does not decay: the pole $\lambda = 0$ has eigenvector $v = (1, 0, 0)$, and the other two modes die away (their poles are $-1.219$ and $-3.281$). So the final state is $\left(w^{\top}x(0)\right)v$, where $w^{\top}$ is the left eigenvector with $w^{\top}A = 0$ and $w^{\top}v = 1$.

Write $w^{\top}A = 0$ column by column. The first column of $A$ is zero, so it gives $0 = 0$. The second column $(1, -0.5, -2)$ gives $w_1 - 0.5w_2 - 2w_3 = 0$. The third column $(0, 1, -4)$ gives $w_2 - 4w_3 = 0$.
The final angle is $w^{\top}x(0) = 1 \times 0 + 1 \times 1 + 0.25 \times 2 = 1.5$. In words: a speed of 1 carries the angle 1 further (the current, which would add 0.25 per unit, adds another 0.5).

blocks.title: Step response of the tanks
blocks.text: Three tanks have $G(s) = 0.6/((s + 1)(s + 0.6)(s + 0.3))$. Find the level of tank 3 five seconds after a unit step of inflow.
solution: Split into partial fractions, $G(s) = \dfrac{c_1}{s + 1} + \dfrac{c_2}{s + 0.6} + \dfrac{c_3}{s + 0.3}$. Each $c$ is found by covering its factor and putting $s$ at its pole in what is left.

A unit step multiplies $G$ by $1/s$. The inverse transform of $c/(s(s + p))$ is $(c/p)(1 - e^{-pt})$, so $y(t) = \dfrac{2.143}{1}(1 - e^{-t}) + \dfrac{-5}{0.6}(1 - e^{-0.6t}) + \dfrac{2.857}{0.3}(1 - e^{-0.3t})$. The constants $2.143 - 8.333 + 9.524 = 3.333$ are $G(0)$.

blocks.title: Why three equal lags are slower
blocks.text: For $G(s) = 1/(s + 1)^3$ (the chain of three lags), check that $A + I$ has only one eigenvector, and find the step response at $t = 2$. Compare it with a single lag $1/(s + 1)$ at $t = 2$.
solution: $A + I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -3 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$. Its first two rows are independent, and the third is $-1\times$ row 1 $-2\times$ row 2: the rank is 2, so $(A + I)v = 0$ has a one-dimensional solution, $v = (1, -1, 1)$. Only one eigen-direction for three poles.

For the response use $e^{At} = e^{-t}(I + tN + \tfrac{t^2}{2}N^2)$. The step response is $y(t) = 1 - e^{-t}(1 + t + t^2/2)$: it is the integral of the impulse response $h(t) = \tfrac12 t^2e^{-t}$. (Integrating by parts twice gives that.)
A single lag: $1 - e^{-2} = 0.865$. The three-lag chain has reached only 32% where the single lag has reached 87%.
blocks.answer: $y(2) = 0.323$, against $0.865$ for one lag; one eigenvector only

blocks.title: Reducing the tanks to one pole
blocks.text: Replace the three tanks by a first-order system that keeps the slowest pole and the steady-state gain $3.333$. Compare its step response at $t = 5$ and $t = 10$ with the exact $1.609$ and $2.880$, and say what is missing.
solution: Keep $s = -0.3$ and demand $G_{\text{red}}(0) = 3.333$: $G_{\text{red}} = \dfrac{3.333 \times 0.3}{s + 0.3} = \dfrac{1}{s + 0.3}$. Its step response is $3.333(1 - e^{-0.3t})$.

Compared with the exact $1.609$ and $2.880$, the reduced model is early: errors of $0.98$ and $0.29$. The reduction forgot the lags of the two fast poles, whose time constants are $1$ s and $1.67$ s. A rough correction is to delay the reduced response by their sum, $1 + 1.67 = 2.67$ s: $3.333(1 - e^{-0.3 \times 2.33}) = 1.678$ at $t = 5$ and $3.333(1 - e^{-0.3 \times 7.33}) = 2.964$ at $t = 10$.

The delayed version is close at $t = 5$ (1.678 against 1.609) and not bad at $t = 10$ (2.964 against 2.880). So the dominant pole fixes where the response ends up and how fast it settles, and the fast poles contribute a delay.
blocks.answer: $2.590$ and $3.167$ (too early); with a $2.67$ s delay $1.678$ and $2.964$
